content.paragraph: Just as we defined single integrals for functions of one variable and double integrals for functions of two variables, so we can define triple integrals for functions of three variables.

subsection.paragraph: Now we define the triple integral over a general bounded region $$\mathbf{E}$$ in three-dimensional space (a solid) by much the same procedure that we used for double integrals (15.2.2). We enclose $$E$$ in a box $$B$$ of the type given by Equation 1. Then we define $$F$$ so that it agrees with $$f$$ on $$E$$ but is $$0$$ for points in $$B$$ that are outside $$E$$ . By definition,

The most difficult step in evaluating a triple integral is setting up an expression for the region of integration (such as Equation 9 in Example 2). Remember that the limits of integration in the inner integral contain at most two variables, the limits of integration in the middle integral contain at most one variable, and the limits of integration in the outer integral must be constants.

subsection.title: Changing the Order of Integration
subsection.paragraph: Fubini’s Theorem for Triple Integrals allows us to express a triple integral as an iterated integral, and there are six different orders of integration in which we can do this. Given an iterated integral, it may be advantageous to change the order of integration because evaluating an iterated integral in one order may be simpler than in another. In the next example we investigate equivalent iterated integrals using different orders of integration.

subsection.title: Applications of Triple Integrals
subsection.paragraph: Recall that if $$f(x) \geqslant 0$$ , then the single integral $${\int_{a}^{b}f}{(x)}\mathit{dx}$$ represents the area under the curve $$y = f(x)$$ from $$a$$ to $$b$$ , and if $$f\left( {x,y} \right) \geqslant 0$$ , then the double integral $${\iint_{D}f}\left( {x,y} \right)\mathit{dA}$$ represents the volume under the surface $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and above $$D$$ . The corresponding interpretation of a triple integral $${\iiint_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}$$ , where $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) \geqslant 0$$ , is not very useful because it would be the “hypervolume” of a four-dimensional object and, of course, that is very difficult to visualize. (Remember that $$E$$ is just the domain of the function $$f$$ ; the graph of $$f$$ lies in four-dimensional space.) Nonetheless, the triple integral $${\iiint_{E}f}{\left( {x,y,z} \right)}\mathit{dV}$$ can be interpreted in different ways in different physical situations, depending on the physical interpretations of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , $$z$$ , and $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ .
Let’s begin with the special case where $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 1$$ for all points in $$E$$ . Then the triple integral does represent the volume of $$E$$ :
For example, you can see this in the case of a type 1 region by putting $$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 1$$ in Formula 6:
and from Section 15.2 we know this represents the volume that lies between the surfaces $$z = u_{1}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and $$z = u_{2}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ .

subsection.paragraph: All the applications of double integrals in Section 15.4 can be extended to triple integrals using analogous reasoning. For example, suppose that a solid object occupying a region $$E$$ has density $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ , in units of mass per unit volume, at each point $$\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ in $$E$$ . To find the total mass $$m$$ of $$E$$ we divide a rectangular box $$B$$ containing $$E$$ into subboxes $$B_{ijk}$$ of the same size (as in Figure 18), and consider $$\rho\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ to be $$0$$ outside $$E$$ . If we choose a point $${({x_{ijk}^{*},y_{ijk}^{*},z_{ijk}^{*}})}\Delta V$$ in $$B_{ijk}$$ , then the mass of the part of $$E$$ that occupies $$B_{ijk}$$ is approximately $$\rho{({x_{ijk}^{*},y_{ijk}^{*},z_{ijk}^{*}})}\Delta V$$ , where $$\Delta V$$ is the volume of $$B_{ijk}$$ .
